meta.framing: How do art historians settle whether a disputed painting is an autograph work by a celebrated master or the product of a workshop assistant or later forger when stylistic connoisseurship, provenance records, and scientific pigment analysis appear to point toward different conclusions?

response:
Disputes over autograph status are rarely settled by any single method. They are settled by weighing connoisseurship, documentation and material evidence against one another until one account explains all of them. A Flemish panel recently reassessed by a museum shows how this works. Although a leading connoisseur judged the brushwork of the faces to be characteristic of the master's own hand, a rival connoisseur argued that the drapery passages were painted by a workshop assistant. The rival's case gains weight from the conditions of production in the period. Seventeenth-century Flemish masters commonly employed assistants to execute parts of their paintings, and that studio custom indicates that a divided execution is the expected case rather than the exceptional one. The disagreement between the two connoisseurs was settled when the museum's attribution review board concluded that the drapery passages were painted by a workshop assistant. That verdict leaves the faces to the master and assigns the drapery to the studio, so the two judgments no longer compete. The board's conclusion was also the cause of that widespread custom of delegation among the Flemish masters.

The physical support provides a second line of inquiry, one that does not depend on judgments of style. The painting is executed on an oak panel; in other words, its support is a board made of oak wood. Material of this kind can be examined by methods that stand entirely apart from questions of brushwork. Dendrochronological analysis dated the felling of the panel's oak to the early seventeenth century. That date sets a lower limit for when the panel could have been painted, and it agrees with the master's working life without proving his authorship. By contrast, dendrochronology can date the linen threads of a canvas support, so the same discipline would have yielded evidence of a different kind had the work been painted on cloth. A felling date therefore narrows the question but does not close it, because an old panel can be reused by a later hand.

Pigment analysis addresses the possibility of forgery most directly, since a forger cannot easily obtain the materials of an earlier century. Either the painting contains no pigment introduced after 1650, or the painting contains at least one pigment introduced after 1650; the two cannot both be true, and one of them must hold. Set against the first of these possibilities, Prussian blue was available to painters in the early sixteenth century, and its history therefore offers no fixed boundary of the kind that later synthetic pigments supply. The interpretive difficulty lies less in detecting a late material than in explaining how it got there. Retouching applied during later restorations can introduce modern pigments into an old painting. That well-documented mechanism is the evidence on which the technical examination's final report determined that the modern pigments were confined to later restoration retouching. It follows that their presence says nothing about the original campaign of painting.

Provenance completes the inquiry, though in this case it is the least decisive strand. The provenance records contain a gap of roughly eighty years in the nineteenth century. At least one of two events, perhaps both, came after that gap opened: the painting left its documented collection through wartime looting during the provenance gap, or the painting changed hands through an unrecorded private sale during the provenance gap. Neither scenario implicates the painter, and neither excludes him. A silent archive is a common condition of old pictures rather than a sign of fabrication. For this reason, art historians treat provenance as corroborating or weakening an attribution reached on other grounds. The panel's case shows the general procedure. Each method answers a narrower question than it first appears to: who painted which passages, when the support was cut, which materials are original, and where the object travelled. The attribution is secure only when a single account answers all four questions at once.
